title: Functional Groups III: Carbonyl Compounds
summary: This lesson introduces the main carbonyl functional groups—aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, and amides—covers their IUPAC naming rules, and explains their characteristic reactions. Students will learn to identify, name, and predict the behavior of these compounds in basic organic transformations.
objectives: Identify the structural formula of aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, and amides
Name each carbonyl compound correctly using IUPAC rules
Describe the key reactions: oxidation of aldehydes, nucleophilic addition to ketones, esterification, and amide formation
Predict the products of simple carbonyl reactions given reactants
Explain how carbonyl groups affect physical properties and reactivity
prerequisites: Students should already know basic covalent bonding, functional group notation, and how to name simple alkanes and alcohols.
why: Carbonyl compounds are found in everyday materials such as sugars, fats, fragrances, and pharmaceuticals. Understanding their chemistry helps explain how food flavors develop, how medicines are made, and how polymers are synthesized.

The reactions of carbonyl groups form the foundation for many industrial processes, from making plastics (esters) to producing polymers like nylon (amides). Mastery of these concepts prepares students for advanced studies in biochemistry, materials science, and drug design.

sections.heading: What is a Carbonyl Group?
sections.body:
The carbonyl group is one of the most important building blocks in organic chemistry.  
It is simply a carbon atom that is double‑bonded to an oxygen atom, written as **C=O**.  
Think of the carbon as a person holding two hands tightly together with the oxygen – the “double bond’’ means the two atoms share two pairs of electrons.

> **Definition:** A carbonyl functional group consists of a carbon atom double‑bonded to an oxygen atom (C=O).  

In a carbonyl compound the carbon is attached to the rest of the molecule by single bonds.  
Because the carbon already shares two pairs of electrons with oxygen, it has only four electrons in its outer shell that are involved in bonding. This leaves the carbon **electron‑poor**, or **electrophilic** – it wants to attract electrons from other atoms or groups.

Why does the double bond make the carbon electrophilic?  
Oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon; it pulls electron density toward itself. In a double bond, oxygen pulls on **both** pairs of shared electrons, pulling the shared electron cloud away from the carbon. The result is a partial positive charge (δ⁺) on the carbon and a partial negative charge (δ⁻) on the oxygen. This separation of charge is called **polarization**.

> **Note:** The carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge (δ⁺) because the attached oxygen pulls electron density toward itself.  

Because of this polarity, the carbonyl carbon behaves like a tiny magnet that attracts nucleophiles – species that have a pair of electrons to donate. Nucleophiles can attack the carbon, forming a new bond while the double bond to oxygen temporarily becomes a single bond. After the attack, the oxygen often regains its double bond by losing a proton or another leaving group. This pattern underlies most reactions of aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, and amides.

An everyday comparison helps: imagine a child (the carbon) holding a heavy backpack (the oxygen). The backpack pulls the child’s weight forward, making the child lean forward (partial positive charge). If someone (a nucleophile) pushes the child from behind, the child moves forward and the backpack may shift its position. In chemistry, the “push’’ is the donation of a pair of electrons to the carbonyl carbon.

The general structure of a carbonyl compound can be drawn as:

$$
\mathrm{R_1\!-\!C(=O)\!-\!R_2}
$$

Here **R₁** and **R₂** represent any groups attached to the carbonyl carbon. They can be hydrogen atoms, alkyl chains, aromatic rings, or other functional groups. Changing R₁ and R₂ gives us different families of carbonyl compounds:

* If one of the R groups is hydrogen (R₁ = H) and the other is any carbon‑containing group, the molecule is an **aldehyde**.  
* If both R groups are carbon‑containing, the molecule is a **ketone**.  
* If one of the R groups is an –OH (hydroxyl) attached to the carbonyl carbon, we have a **carboxylic acid**.  
* If the –OH is replaced by an –OR group (where R is an alkyl), the compound is an **ester**.  
* If the –OH is replaced by an –NR₂ group (where N is nitrogen), the compound is an **amide**.

All of these share the same C=O core, and therefore all show the same electrophilic character at the carbonyl carbon. Recognizing the carbonyl group lets you predict how a molecule will behave in a reaction, which is why chemists memorize its shape and polarity early on.

> **Remember:** The double bond to oxygen pulls electron density away from carbon, giving the carbonyl carbon a partial positive charge and making it a prime target for nucleophilic attack.  

Understanding this simple idea – a carbon atom double‑bonded to an oxygen atom, polarized, and ready to accept electrons – is the foundation for everything that follows in carbonyl chemistry. Once you can spot the C=O group on a structure, you can start to guess how the molecule will react, what products might form, and how to name it correctly.

sections.heading: Aldehydes and Ketones
sections.body:
Aldehydes and ketones are the two most common families of carbonyl compounds.  
Both contain the carbonyl group — a carbon atom double‑bonded to an oxygen atom (C=O).  
The difference lies in what is attached to the carbonyl carbon.

**Aldehyde**  
The carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen atom. Its general formula is  

$$\text{R–CHO}$$  

where **R** represents any carbon‑containing chain (which may be a simple alkyl group or a more complex substituent). The “CHO” part tells us that the carbonyl carbon carries a hydrogen (the “H”) and the double‑bonded oxygen (the “O”).

**Ketone**  
The carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon groups and never to hydrogen. Its general formula is  

$$\text{R–CO–R'}$$  

Here **R** and **R'** are each carbon chains that can be the same or different. The carbonyl carbon sits between them, so the group is often called a “C‑O‑C” bridge.

> **Definition:** An aldehyde has the structure R‑CHO (hydrogen attached to the carbonyl carbon); a ketone has the structure R‑CO‑R′ (two carbon groups attached to the carbonyl carbon).

---

### Naming the compounds  

1. **Identify the longest carbon chain that contains the carbonyl carbon.**  
   This chain determines the base name.  

2. **For aldehydes**  
   * Add the suffix **‑al** to the parent hydrocarbon name.  
   * If the aldehyde group is not at the end of the longest chain, give the carbon bearing the –CHO group the lowest possible number and write it as a prefix “formyl‑”.  
   * Example: CH₃CH₂CHO → *propanal* (three‑carbon chain, aldehyde at the end).  

3. **For ketones**  
   * Add the suffix **‑one** to the parent name.  
   * Number the chain so that the carbonyl carbon gets the lowest possible number; write that number before the suffix.  
   * Example: CH₃COCH₂CH₃ → *butan‑2‑one* (four‑carbon chain, carbonyl on carbon 2).  

> **Note:** Do not use “‑al” for ketones or “‑one” for aldehydes; the suffix tells you which family the molecule belongs to.

---

### Why the carbonyl group matters  

The carbonyl carbon is **electrophilic** – it loves electrons because the double bond to oxygen pulls electron density away, leaving the carbon partially positive.  
When a molecule that can donate a pair of electrons (a **nucleophile**) approaches, it can add to the carbonyl carbon. This is called a **nucleophilic addition reaction**.  

In everyday life, think of the carbonyl carbon as a “magnet” that attracts electron‑rich guests. Aldehydes are a bit more “magnetic” than ketones because the attached hydrogen does not donate electron density, so aldehydes react faster in many addition reactions.

---

### General pattern of nucleophilic addition  

1. **Nucleophile attacks** the carbonyl carbon, forming a new single bond.  
2. **π‑bond (the C=O double bond) breaks**, and the oxygen takes the electrons, becoming an **alkoxide ion** (a negatively charged oxygen).  

The overall transformation can be written as  

$$\text{R–C(=O)–R'} + \text{Nu}^- \;\longrightarrow\; \text{R–C(–Nu)(–O}^-\text{)–R'}$$  

where **Nu⁻** stands for any nucleophile (e.g., $ \text{CN}^- $, $ \text{H}^- $, $ \text{H}_2\text{O} $).  

After the addition, the alkoxide ion is usually **protonated** (receives a hydrogen ion, $ \text{H}^+ $) from water or an acid to give the neutral product.  

> **Remember:** The key steps are attack on the carbonyl carbon, breaking of the C=O π‑bond, and final protonation of the oxygen.

---

### Typical nucleophiles for aldehydes and ketones  

| Nucleophile | Typical product (after protonation) | Example reaction |
|-------------|--------------------------------------|------------------|
| Hydride ion $ \text{H}^- $ (from NaBH₄, LiAlH₄) | Alcohol (primary from aldehyde, secondary from ketone) | $$\text{R–CHO} + \text{H}^- \rightarrow \text{R–CH}_2\text{OH}$$ |
| Cyanide $ \text{CN}^- $ | Cyanohydrin (contains –OH and –CN) | $$\text{R–CO–R'} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{R–C(OH)(CN)–R'}$$ |
| Water $ \text{H}_2\text{O} $ (acidic conditions) | Gem‑diol (two –OH on the same carbon, usually unstable) | $$\text{R–CHO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{R–C(OH)_2}$$ |

These reactions are the foundation for many synthetic steps in organic chemistry, allowing us to turn a simple carbonyl into a wide variety of functional groups.

> **In daily life:** Aldehydes give the pleasant smell of fresh cut grass (hexanal) and the scent of cinnamon (cinnamaldehyde). Ketones are responsible for the fruity aroma of acetone in nail polish remover. Their reactivity with nucleophiles is why they are useful in making flavors, fragrances, and pharmaceuticals.

sections.heading: Carboxylic Acids
sections.body:
The carbonyl group is a carbon atom double‑bonded to an oxygen atom ($\ce{C=O}$).  
When a hydroxyl group ($\ce{-OH}$) is attached directly to that same carbon, the whole fragment is called a **carboxyl group**, written as $ \ce{-COOH} $.  

> **Definition:** A carboxylic acid is any organic molecule that contains the $ \ce{-COOH} $ group.

---

### Why the $ \ce{-COOH} $ group makes the molecule acidic  

In water, the $ \ce{-COOH} $ group can lose a hydrogen ion (a proton, $\ce{H+}$).  
The loss looks like this:

$$\ce{R-COOH -> R-COO- + H+}$$  

The remaining part, $ \ce{R-COO-} $, is called a **carboxylate ion**.  
The reason this proton leaves easily is that the negative charge that forms after loss is spread over two oxygen atoms. This spreading, called **resonance**, stabilises the ion and makes the original acid stronger than, for example, an alcohol ($\ce{R-OH}$) where the charge would sit on a single oxygen.

> **Note:** The resonance structures of the carboxylate ion are  
> $$\ce{R-C(=O)O- \leftrightarrow R-C(-O)O=}$$  
> showing the negative charge shared between the two oxygens.

Because the proton can leave readily, carboxylic acids have typical pKa values around 4–5, meaning they are much stronger acids than most other organic compounds.

---

### Naming carboxylic acids (IUPAC rules)

1. **Find the longest carbon chain that includes the carbonyl carbon** (the carbon of the $ \ce{C=O} $).  
2. **Number the chain so that the carbonyl carbon gets the lowest possible number.**  
3. **Replace the ending of the parent alkane name with “‑carboxylic acid.”**  
   - For a three‑carbon chain, the parent alkane is propane; the acid is **propanoic acid**.  
   - If there are substituents, name them as usual and give their positions, e.g., **2‑methylbutanoic acid**.

If the acid is very common, a trivial name may be used (e.g., acetic acid for ethanoic acid, benzoic acid for benzoic acid).  

> **Remember:** The “‑oic acid” suffix always tells you that a $ \ce{-COOH} $ group is present at the end of the chain.

---

### Acid‑catalyzed dehydration: turning an alcohol into a carbonyl

A useful reaction for making carbonyl compounds from carboxylic acids is **dehydration** (removing water).  
In the presence of a strong acid such as sulfuric acid ($\ce{H2SO4}$), the hydroxyl group of the $ \ce{-COOH} $ can be protonated, turning it into a better leaving group ($\ce{-OH2+}$). Water then leaves, and the remaining oxygen forms a double bond with carbon, giving a carbonyl compound called an **acid anhydride** if two acid molecules combine, or a **ketone** if the acid is first converted to an acyl chloride and then reacts with a carbonyl‑nucleophile.

A simple example is the formation of **acetic anhydride** from two molecules of acetic acid:

$$\ce{2 CH3COOH -> (CH3CO)2O + H2O}$$  

The steps are:

1. **Protonation:** $\ce{CH3COOH + H+ -> CH3C(OH)2+}$  
2. **Loss of water:** $\ce{CH3C(OH)2+ -> CH3CO+ + H2O}$ (the acylium ion)  
3. **Attack by another acid molecule:** $\ce{CH3CO+ + CH3COOH -> (CH3CO)2O + H+}$  

The acid catalyst is regenerated in the last step, so only a small amount is needed.

> **In daily life:** Acetic anhydride is used to make acetylated flavors and pharmaceuticals; the same dehydration idea is used when making polyester fibers from dicarboxylic acids and diols.

---

### Key take‑aways

- The $ \ce{-COOH} $ group is a carbonyl ($\ce{C=O}$) attached to a hydroxyl ($\ce{-OH}$).  
- Its acidity comes from resonance‑stabilised carboxylate ions after losing a proton.  
- IUPAC names end in “‑oic acid” and are built on the longest chain that includes the carbonyl carbon.  
- Acid‑catalyzed dehydration removes water and can link two acid molecules, forming anhydrides or other carbonyl derivatives.  

Understanding these points lets you recognise carboxylic acids in formulas, name them correctly, and predict how they behave in common laboratory reactions.

sections.heading: Esters
sections.body:
Esters are a special type of carbonyl compound that look like **R‑COO‑R'**.  
The “R” and “R’” each stand for a carbon‑containing group such as a chain of atoms (for example, CH₃‑ or C₂H₅‑). The central part **‑COO‑** is what makes an ester different from other carbonyl groups.

> **Definition:** An ester is a molecule that contains the functional group **‑COO‑** attached to two carbon groups (R and R’).

### How an ester is formed  

Think of a carboxylic acid as a “parent” molecule that has a carbonyl group (C=O) and a hydroxyl group (‑OH) attached to the same carbon:  

$$\text{R‑COOH}$$  

If we replace the hydrogen of the hydroxyl group (the “H” in ‑OH) with another carbon group, we get an ester. This replacement is called **esterification**. The reaction usually needs an acid catalyst (often sulfuric acid) and heat:

$$\text{R‑COOH} + \text{R'‑OH} \;\xrightarrow{\text{H⁺, heat}}\; \text{R‑COO‑R'} + \text{H₂O}$$  

In words: a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol (R'‑OH) to give an ester (R‑COO‑R') and water. The water molecule is a **by‑product** that is removed to drive the reaction forward.

> **Note:** Removing the water (for example, by using a Dean‑Stark trap) pushes the equilibrium toward more ester formation.

### Naming an ester  

The name of an ester is built from the two carbon groups:

1. **Name the part that comes from the alcohol (R')** – treat it as if it were an alkane, then change the ending **‑ane** to **‑yl**.  
   *Example:* CH₃CH₂‑ becomes **ethyl**.

2. **Name the part that comes from the acid (R‑CO‑)** – drop the **‑OH** from the acid name and keep the **‑oic acid** ending, but replace **‑oic** with **‑ate**.  
   *Example:* CH₃COOH (acetic acid) becomes **acetate**.

Combine them as **[alcohol‑derived name] [acid‑derived name]**.  
So CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ is called **ethyl acetate**.

> **In daily life:** Ethyl acetate smells fruity and is used as a nail‑polish remover and a flavoring agent. The pleasant smell of many fruits comes from esters such as isoamyl acetate (banana scent).

### Why esters are useful  

Esters are less acidic than the carboxylic acids they come from, so they do not donate protons easily. This makes them good solvents for many organic reactions. Their pleasant aromas also make them valuable in perfumes, food flavorings, and even in some medicines.

### Hydrolysis – breaking the ester back down  

If we add water to an ester in the presence of acid or a base, the ester can be split again into a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. This is called **hydrolysis** (literally “water‑splitting”).

*Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis*:

$$\text{R‑COO‑R'} + \text{H₂O} \;\xrightarrow{\text{H⁺}}\; \text{R‑COOH} + \text{R'‑OH}$$  

*Base‑catalyzed hydrolysis* (often called **saponification** because it is the basis of soap making):

$$\text{R‑COO‑R'} + \text{OH⁻} \;\rightarrow\; \text{R‑COO⁻} + \text{R'‑OH}$$  

The carboxylate ion (R‑COO⁻) can then combine with a metal cation (like Na⁺) to give a soap molecule.

> **Remember:** In acid hydrolysis the products are the original acid and alcohol; in base hydrolysis the acid becomes a carboxylate salt, which is why soaps are salty, water‑soluble compounds.

### Small checklist for working with esters  

- **Identify** the carbonyl carbon (the one double‑bonded to oxygen) and the adjacent oxygen that links to R’.  
- **Write** the esterification equation, making sure the water molecule appears on the product side.  
- **Name** the ester by first naming the alcohol‑derived part (‑yl) then the acid‑derived part (‑ate).  
- **Predict** the products of hydrolysis: acid + alcohol (acid) or carboxylate + alcohol (base).  

Understanding how esters are built from carboxylic acids, how they are named, and how they interconvert through esterification and hydrolysis gives you a solid foundation for many reactions you will meet later in organic chemistry.

sections.heading: Amides
sections.body:
Amides are a special family of carbonyl compounds that contain the group **‑C(=O)‑NH₂**, **‑C(=O)‑NHR**, or **‑C(=O)‑NR₂**.  
In plain words, an amide is a carbonyl (a carbon double‑bonded to oxygen) that is also bonded to a nitrogen atom. The nitrogen may carry two hydrogens (‑CONH₂), one hydrogen and one carbon chain (‑CONHR), or two carbon chains (‑CONR₂).  

> **Definition:** An amide is any molecule that has the functional group –C(=O)–NR₂, where R can be hydrogen or an alkyl/aryl group.

Why does this matter? The carbon‑oxygen double bond makes the carbon very electrophilic (it wants electrons), while the attached nitrogen can donate its lone pair of electrons. This combination gives amides a distinctive stability and reactivity that is useful in biology (proteins are made of amide bonds) and in many synthetic materials such as nylon.

### How amides are named (IUPAC)

The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) gives systematic names to amides. The basic steps are:

1. **Identify the longest carbon chain that contains the carbonyl carbon.** This chain becomes the parent “alkane” name (e.g., “pentane” for five carbons).  
2. **Replace the ending “‑ane” with “‑amide”.** So a five‑carbon chain gives “pentanamide”.  
3. **If the nitrogen carries substituents, list them as prefixes before the parent name.**  
   * Example: CH₃‑C(=O)‑NH‑CH₃ is named *N‑methyl‑ethanamide* (the parent chain has two carbons, “ethan‑”, and the nitrogen has one methyl group, “N‑methyl”).  
4. **If the carbon chain itself has substituents, name them as usual (e.g., “3‑chloro‑butanamide”).**  

> **Note:** The “N‑” prefix tells you that the substituent is attached to the nitrogen, not to the carbonyl carbon.

### Making amides from carboxylic acids and amines

Amides are most commonly prepared by a condensation reaction between a **carboxylic acid** (a molecule with the group –C(=O)OH) and an **amine** (a molecule with the group –NH₂, –NHR, or –NR₂). The word *condensation* means that two molecules join together while a small molecule, usually water, is lost.

The overall reaction looks like this:

$$
\text{R‑COOH} + \text{R'‑NH₂} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{R‑C(=O)‑NHR'} + \text{H₂O}
$$

Step‑by‑step explanation:

1. **Activation of the acid:** The carbonyl carbon of the acid is already electrophilic, but the –OH group is a poor leaving group. Heating or using a coupling agent (like DCC) makes the –OH leave more easily.  
2. **Nucleophilic attack:** The lone pair on the nitrogen of the amine attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.  
3. **Elimination of water:** The intermediate collapses, expelling a molecule of water and re‑forming the carbonyl double bond, now attached to nitrogen – the amide bond.  

Because water is produced, the reaction is reversible. Removing water (by drying agents or by using a large excess of one reactant) pushes the equilibrium toward the amide product.

> **In daily life:** The protein fibers in your hair and nails are linked together by amide bonds, often called peptide bonds. This is why cutting hair with scissors breaks many amide links, but the overall structure stays strong.

### Small variations

- **Primary amides** (‑CONH₂) come from ammonia (NH₃) reacting with a carboxylic acid.  
- **Secondary amides** (‑CONHR) use a primary amine (RNH₂).  
- **Tertiary amides** (‑CONR₂) need a secondary amine (R₂NH).  

Each step reduces the number of hydrogens attached to nitrogen, which slightly changes the basicity and solubility of the product.

> **Remember:** In an amide, the nitrogen’s lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl group, making the C‑N bond partially double‑bond character. This delocalization is why amides are less basic than free amines and why they are relatively resistant to hydrolysis under mild conditions.

sections.heading: Key Reactions of Carbonyl Compounds
sections.body:
A carbonyl group ($\mathrm{C=O}$) is a carbon atom double‑bonded to an oxygen atom. Because the oxygen pulls electron density toward itself, the carbon becomes **electrophilic** – it likes to accept electrons from a partner. This simple fact makes carbonyl compounds very reactive and gives us a toolbox of useful reactions.

> **Definition:** *Electrophilic* means “electron‑loving”. The carbon of a carbonyl wants a pair of electrons to fill its bond, so other molecules that can donate a pair will attack it.

---

### 1. Oxidation of Aldehydes to Carboxylic Acids  

An aldehyde has the formula $\mathrm{R–CHO}$. The carbonyl carbon already has one hydrogen attached. If we add an oxidizing agent (something that takes electrons away), that hydrogen is removed and another oxygen is added, giving a carboxylic acid $\mathrm{R–COOH}$.

$$\mathrm{R–CHO \xrightarrow[\,\text{acidic}\,]{\text{oxidiser}} R–COOH}$$  

Why does this happen? Oxidation means the carbon loses electrons; the hydrogen is taken away as a proton ($\mathrm{H^+}$) and the carbon gains an extra oxygen atom, forming the –COOH group. In the laboratory, common oxidisers are potassium permanganate ($\mathrm{KMnO_4}$) or chromium(VI) reagents.

> **In daily life:** The smell of a fresh orange peel comes from aldehydes. When the peel ages, those aldehydes are slowly oxidised to acids, which give the rind its sour taste.

---

### 2. Nucleophilic Addition to Aldehydes and Ketones  

A *nucleophile* is a species that donates a pair of electrons (the opposite of electrophile). Because the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic, a nucleophile can add to it. The first step is the nucleophile attacking the carbon, opening the double bond and creating a tetrahedral intermediate. Then a proton is transferred to give the final product.

General form (using a generic nucleophile $\mathrm{Nu^-}$):

$$\mathrm{R_2C=O + Nu^- \rightarrow R_2C(ONu)H}$$  

For example, adding water ($\mathrm{H_2O}$) to a ketone gives a *hydrate*:

$$\mathrm{R_2C=O + H_2O \rightarrow R_2C(OH)_2}$$  

Why is this useful? Many important transformations—such as forming alcohols, cyanohydrins, or imines—start with this simple addition step.

> **Note:** Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes because the carbonyl carbon in a ketone is surrounded by two alkyl groups that donate electron density, making it a bit less electrophilic.

---

### 3. Fischer Esterification  

An *ester* is a carbonyl compound where the carbonyl carbon is bonded to an –OR group instead of –OH. Fischer esterification is a classic way to make esters from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol. The reaction needs an acid catalyst (often sulfuric acid) and heat.

$$\mathrm{R–COOH + R'–OH \xrightarrow[\text{heat}]{\text{H^+}} R–COOR' + H_2O}$$  

Step‑by‑step:  
1. The acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon even more electrophilic.  
2. The alcohol attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.  
3. A proton transfer rearranges the intermediate, and water leaves, restoring the carbonyl double bond and giving the ester.

Why learn this? Esters smell fruity and are used in flavors, perfumes, and as solvents. The reaction also illustrates how we can swap the –OH of an acid for an –OR group.

> **Common mistake:** Forgetting to remove water (or use excess alcohol) drives the equilibrium backward, giving low ester yield. Removing water shifts the reaction toward product formation.

---

### 4. Amide Synthesis (From Acid Chlorides)  

An *amide* has the structure $\mathrm{R–C(=O)–NR_2}$. One reliable laboratory route is to start with an acid chloride ($\mathrm{R–COCl}$) and react it with an amine ($\mathrm{R'NH_2}$). The chloride is a very good leaving group, so the amine attacks the carbonyl carbon and displaces chloride.

$$\mathrm{R–COCl + R'NH_2 \rightarrow R–C(=O)–NR' + HCl}$$  

The reaction is fast because the carbonyl carbon in an acid chloride is highly electrophilic. The by‑product hydrogen chloride ($\mathrm{HCl}$) is usually trapped by a base (e.g., pyridine) to keep the mixture neutral.

Why is this important? Amides are the backbone of proteins (the peptide bond) and appear in many polymers and drugs. Understanding their formation helps students see the link between simple organic reactions and biology.

> **Remember:** Always use a base to neutralize the $\mathrm{HCl}$ formed; otherwise the amine can become protonated and lose its nucleophilicity.

---

These four reactions—oxidation, nucleophilic addition, Fischer esterification, and amide synthesis—show how the carbonyl’s electrophilic carbon can be transformed in many useful ways. By recognizing the carbonyl as a “sticky” spot for electron‑rich partners, you can predict how a wide variety of reagents will change the molecule, just as you would anticipate how a magnet attracts iron filings. Practice drawing the arrows and balancing each step, and the patterns will become second nature.

sections.heading: Practice: Naming and Predicting Products
sections.body:
When you look at a picture of a molecule, the first thing you should do is **name** it.  
Naming tells you exactly which atoms are where, and it lets you compare one compound to another.  
After you know the name, you can think about how the molecule will behave in a reaction.  
The two skills—naming and predicting products—go hand‑in‑hand, just like reading a recipe and then cooking the dish.

Below are short practice problems.  
Each problem has two parts:

1. **Name the structure** (use IUPAC rules for aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, esters, and amides).  
2. **Predict the major product** of the reaction shown.  

Work through them step‑by‑step. Write the name first, then draw the product. If you get stuck, remember the key ideas from the earlier lessons:

* Aldehyde carbonyl carbon is at the end of the chain → can be oxidized to a carboxylic acid.  
* Ketone carbonyl carbon is inside the chain → cannot be oxidized further without breaking the chain.  
* Carboxylic acids can lose water to form esters (Fischer esterification).  
* Esters can be reduced to aldehydes (DIBAL‑H) or alcohols (LiAlH₄).  
* Amides are very stable; strong acid or base is needed to hydrolyze them back to acids or amines.

---

### Exercise 1 – Aldehyde Naming & Oxidation

**Structure:**  

```
CH3‑CH2‑CH2‑CHO
```

**Reaction:** Treat with $ \text{KMnO}_4 $ (acidic, warm).

1. **Name the compound.**  
2. **Predict the major product** after oxidation.

> **Remember:** Aldehydes are easily oxidized to carboxylic acids; the carbonyl carbon stays in the same place.

---

### Exercise 2 – Ketone Naming & Nucleophilic Addition

**Structure:**  

```
   O
   ||
CH3‑C‑CH2‑CH3
```

**Reaction:** Add $ \text{NaBH}_4 $ in methanol.

1. **Name the compound.**  
2. **Predict the major product** after reduction.

> **Note:** $ \text{NaBH}_4 $ is a mild reducing agent that converts ketones to secondary alcohols without touching esters or acids.

---

### Exercise 3 – Carboxylic Acid Naming & Ester Formation

**Structure:**  

```
   O
   ||
HO‑C‑CH2‑CH3
```

**Reaction:** React with excess ethanol ($\text{EtOH}$) and a few drops of sulfuric acid, then remove water.

1. **Name the compound.**  
2. **Predict the major product** (the ester formed).

> **Definition:** Fischer esterification is the reversible reaction where a carboxylic acid and an alcohol combine, losing one molecule of water, to give an ester.

The overall equation is  

$$\text{R‑COOH} + \text{R'‑OH} \;\xrightleftharpoons[\text{remove H}_2\text{O}]{\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4}\; \text{R‑COOR'} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

---

### Exercise 4 – Ester Naming & Reduction to Aldehyde

**Structure:**  

```
   O
   ||
CH3‑C‑O‑CH2‑CH3
```

**Reaction:** Treat with DIBAL‑H (di‑isobutyl‑aluminium‑hydride) at –78 °C, then quench with water.

1. **Name the compound.**  
2. **Predict the major product** after the reduction.

> **Common mistake:** Using a strong reducing agent like LiAlH₄ would give an alcohol instead of an aldehyde. DIBAL‑H at low temperature stops at the aldehyde stage.

---

### Exercise 5 – Amide Naming & Hydrolysis

**Structure:**  

```
   O
   ||
CH3‑C‑NH₂
```

**Reaction:** Heat with aqueous HCl (strong acid) for 2 h.

1. **Name the compound.**  
2. **Predict the major product** after acid hydrolysis.

> **In daily life:** This type of reaction is how proteins are broken down into amino acids during digestion.

---

### How to Check Your Answers

1. **Write the IUPAC name** on a piece of paper.  
2. **Identify the functional group** (aldehyde, ketone, etc.).  
3. **Match the reagent** to the rule you learned (oxidation, reduction, esterification, hydrolysis).  
4. **Draw the product** showing any new bonds or lost atoms.  

If the product you drew has the same functional group as the rule predicts, you are correct. If not, revisit the rule and see where the carbonyl carbon moved or what new groups were added.

> **Remember:** Practice makes the naming and predicting steps automatic, just like learning to read a map makes traveling easier. Keep a notebook of these short exercises; the more you solve, the faster you will recognize patterns in carbonyl chemistry.

examples.title: Identify a carbonyl functional group
examples.given: A molecule has the formula CH₃‑CH₂‑C(=O)‑CH₃. State which carbonyl functional group it contains.

steps.label: Locate C=O
steps.text: Find the carbon double‑bonded to oxygen; it is the carbonyl group.

steps.label: Count substituents on carbonyl carbon
steps.text: The carbonyl carbon is attached to two carbon atoms (CH₃‑CH₂‑ and ‑CH₃).

steps.label: Classify
steps.text: A carbonyl carbon attached to two other carbons is a ketone.

examples.answer: The compound contains a ketone functional group (specifically, 2‑butanone).

examples.title: Name an ester from its structure
examples.given: The structure is CH₃‑C(=O)‑O‑CH₂‑CH₃. Provide the IUPAC name of this ester.

steps.label: Identify carbonyl carbon
steps.text: The carbonyl carbon is part of a C=O group attached to an –O‑ substituent.

steps.label: Determine acid part
steps.text: The carbonyl carbon plus the attached carbon chain (CH₃‑C(=O)‑) corresponds to acetic acid → “acetyl”.

steps.label: Assemble name
steps.text: Combine acid and alcohol parts as “ethyl acetate”.

examples.answer: The compound is ethyl acetate (IUPAC name: ethyl ethanoate).

examples.title: Predict the major product of a nucleophilic addition to an aldehyde under acidic conditions
examples.given: 2‑methylpropanal (CH₃‑CH₂‑CH(=O)‑CH₃) reacts with excess HCN in aqueous acid. Identify the major product formed.

steps.label: Recognize carbonyl type
steps.text: The compound is an aldehyde; its carbonyl carbon is electrophilic.

steps.label: Add cyanide nucleophile
steps.text: CN⁻ attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate.

steps.label: Protonate alkoxide
steps.text: In acidic solution, the alkoxide is protonated to give a neutral alcohol.

steps.label: Identify functional group formed
steps.text: The addition of HCN converts the aldehyde into a cyanohydrin (–OH and –CN on the same carbon).

examples.answer: The major product is the cyanohydrin 2‑methyl‑2‑hydroxy‑butanenitrile (CH₃‑CH₂‑C(OH)(CN)‑CH₃).

practice.q: Name the functional group in the molecule CH₃‑CHO.
practice.a: The molecule CH₃‑CHO is an aldehyde. It contains a carbonyl group (C=O) attached to at least one hydrogen atom. The functional group is the **aldehyde** group, –CHO.

practice.q: Predict the major product when acetone (CH₃‑CO‑CH₃) reacts with NaBH₄ in methanol.
practice.a:
NaBH₄ is a reducing agent that adds a hydride (H⁻) to the carbonyl carbon of a ketone.
1. Hydride attacks the carbonyl carbon, breaking the C=O double bond.
2. The oxygen picks up a proton from the solvent (methanol).
Result: the carbonyl becomes an alcohol, giving **2-propanol** (CH₃‑CH(OH)‑CH₃).

practice.q: Write the IUPAC name for the compound CH₃‑CH₂‑C(=O)‑OH.
practice.a:
The skeleton is a three‑carbon chain with a carboxylic acid at carbon‑1.
1. The longest chain containing the –COOH group has three carbons → “propanoic acid”.
2. No substituents are present.
Therefore, the IUPAC name is **propanoic acid**.

practice.q: Predict the product when ethyl acetate (CH₃COOCH₂CH₃) undergoes acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis.
practice.a:
Acid‑catalyzed hydrolysis of an ester yields a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.
1. Protonate the carbonyl oxygen of the ester.
2. Water attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.
3. Collapse of the intermediate expels ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) and regenerates the carbonyl.
4. De‑protonation gives the acid.
Products: **acetic acid (CH₃COOH)** and **ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH)**.

practice.q: Draw and name the product formed when benzaldehyde (C₆H₅‑CHO) reacts with excess NaBH₄ in ethanol, then is oxidized with PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate).
practice.a:
Step 1 – Reduction with NaBH₄:
- NaBH₄ reduces the aldehyde to a primary alcohol.
- Product: benzyl alcohol (C₆H₅‑CH₂OH).
Step 2 – Oxidation with PCC:
- PCC oxidizes primary alcohols to aldehydes (stop at aldehyde).
- Benzyl alcohol is converted back to benzaldehyde.
Overall, the starting material is regenerated; the net product is **benzaldehyde** (C₆H₅‑CHO).

practice.q: A compound with formula C₄H₇NO₂ is known to be an amide. Propose its structure, name it, and show the reaction with aqueous HCl that gives the corresponding carboxylic acid and ammonium chloride.
practice.a:
1. Determine the possible amide:
- An amide has the general formula R‑C(=O)‑NR₂.
- For C₄H₇NO₂, subtract the amide functional group (C=O‑NH₂) → leaves C₃H₅.
- The simplest is **propionamide**: CH₃‑CH₂‑C(=O)‑NH₂.
2. Name: **propionamide** (systematic IUPAC name: propanamide).
3. Reaction with aqueous HCl (hydrolysis):
CH₃‑CH₂‑C(=O)‑NH₂ + H₂O + HCl → CH₃‑CH₂‑COOH + NH₄Cl
- The amide carbonyl is protonated, water attacks, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.
- Collapse releases NH₃, which is immediately protonated by HCl to NH₄⁺, forming NH₄Cl.
- The carbonyl reforms as a carboxylic acid (propionic acid).
Thus, propionamide hydrolyzes to **propionic acid (CH₃CH₂COOH)** and **ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl)**.

recap: Carbonyl compounds contain a carbon double‑bonded to oxygen (C=O). The carbon is electrophilic, making these molecules reactive. Aldehydes have a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, ketones have two carbon groups, carboxylic acids add an OH, esters replace that H with another carbon group, and amides attach a nitrogen.

key_terms.meaning: A carbon atom double‑bonded to an oxygen atom (C=O).
Attracts electrons; the carbonyl carbon seeks electron pairs.
A carbonyl compound where the carbonyl carbon is bonded to at least one hydrogen (R‑CHO).
A carbonyl compound where the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon groups (R‑CO‑R').
A carbonyl compound with a hydroxyl group on the same carbon (‑COOH).
A carbonyl compound where the hydroxyl hydrogen is replaced by a carbon group (R‑COO‑R').
A carbonyl compound where the hydroxyl oxygen is replaced by a nitrogen (‑C(=O)‑NR₂).
Delocalisation of electrons over two or more atoms, stabilising ions such as carboxylates.

quiz.q: Which functional group makes a carbonyl carbon most electrophilic?
quiz.why: The carbonyl carbon in an aldehyde has only one electron‑donating carbon attached, increasing its electrophilicity.

quiz.q: What is the general formula for a ketone?
quiz.why: Ketones have a carbonyl carbon bonded to two carbon groups, written R‑CO‑R'.

quiz.q: In which reaction does an aldehyde become a carboxylic acid?
quiz.why: Oxidation adds an oxygen and removes the aldehyde hydrogen, giving a carboxylic acid.

quiz.q: What is the key stabilising factor for the carboxylate ion?
quiz.why: Resonance spreads the negative charge over two oxygens, stabilising the ion.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes an ester?
options: Carbonyl carbon attached to OH and H
Carbonyl carbon attached to two carbons
quiz.why: Esters have the –COO– group where the oxygen is bonded to a carbon group (–O–R).

quiz.q: Why are amides less reactive than aldehydes toward nucleophiles?
options: The nitrogen donates electron density to the carbonyl
quiz.why: Nitrogen’s lone pair delocalises into the carbonyl, reducing its electrophilicity.
